$description: Which packages `@pacit/components` is allowed to bring into a consumer's tree (req-project-dependencies). Point 7 of `check-package.mjs` reads this file against the PACKED manifest and against the imports of the packed code, in both directions: a name declared without an entry here is a dependency added by reflex, an entry with no dependency behind it is a permit the next reflex slips in under, and an import nobody declared is a package the consumer's install does not bring. The promise is "as few as possible", and no gate can measure "as possible" — what it can measure is that every one of them was written down on purpose, with the reason readable at the place the next one gets added.
$forbidden: There is also a list this file cannot extend: `@angular/animations` and `@angular/platform-browser/animations` are refused by point 7 of `check-package.mjs` (rule `forbidden`) wherever they appear — imported, declared, or written into `allowed` below with the best reason anybody can give (req-api-animations). The ban is in the gate and not in this file on purpose: this is a list of permits, and a refusal standing among permits is one word's edit away from being a permit itself. Point 8 reads the other road to the same runtime, which leaves no name here at all — an animation binding needs no dependency to work in a consumer's application, only in theirs rather than in ours (lesson-87).
$allowed: One entry per package. `name` is the package as it stands in the manifest, `kind` is the field it has to stand in — `peer` for `peerDependencies` (the consumer already has it, and a second copy in their tree is a second injector), `runtime` for `dependencies` (it arrives with the install and weighs something in every application). `reason` says why it is deliberate; it is read by a person, and its absence fires. `unimported` is the exception for a dependency no import in the package can show — it carries its own reason, and without it a dependency nothing imports fires as dead weight. There is deliberately no entry for what the Angular CLI provides to a schematic at `ng add` time (`@angular-devkit/schematics` and its neighbours): today the only schematic imports it as a TYPE, which the compiler erases, so the artefact needs no such rule — and a mechanism with no case behind it is a rule nobody has read.

allowed.name: @angular/compiler
allowed.reason: Angular's own template parser, and the `ng update` migration is the only thing that calls it: `HtmlParser` returns every element and attribute of an `.html` file with its exact span, which is how `badge-tone` stopped keeping a second copy of the lexer and stopped writing where Angular would not (lesson-236). A peer and never a runtime dependency — it is a compiler, it has no business weighing on an application, and every workspace that builds an Angular application already has it, because `@angular/build` requires it as a peer of its own. `peerDependenciesMeta` marks it OPTIONAL, which is the honest shape: the migration reaches it through a dynamic `import()` and treats failure as an answer, writing nowhere and reporting every file worth a look.
allowed.unimported: No bundle imports it and none ever will: the call is a dynamic `import()` inside the schematics tree, which ng-packagr does not build and which ships as CommonJS beside the package. The entry says so out loud, because a dependency the packed code cannot show an import for is otherwise dead weight — here the import exists, in the one file the consumer runs once.

allowed.name: @angular/core
allowed.reason: The framework the components are compiled against. It can be nothing but a peer: a second copy of `@angular/core` in the consumer's tree is a second injector and a second set of the tokens the library resolves through, and the failure it produces reads as a bug in the library.

allowed.name: @angular/common
allowed.reason: `NgTemplateOutlet`, and nothing else — the one piece of the framework that renders a template a consumer handed over (`req-api-templates`, decision 0027). It arrived with the select's option slot at D5 and is a peer for `@angular/core`'s reason rather than a weaker one: `@angular/common` is versioned in lockstep with the framework and a second copy of it is the same second injector. Writing the outlet by hand was the alternative and was refused — the context-update semantics (when an embedded view is rebuilt and when its context is merely rewritten) are the framework's to specify, and a library reimplementing them owns a divergence nobody would see until it misrendered.

allowed.name: @angular/forms
allowed.reason: Signal forms: the controls bind to `Control` and to the field API from `@angular/forms/signals`. The same peer argument as `@angular/core` — a form control from a second copy of the package is a different class than the one the library checks against.

allowed.name: @angular/cdk
allowed.reason: Overlay mechanics and the focus trap — decision 0013 buys the machinery here and keeps the API our own. Two entrypoints, not one: `@angular/cdk/overlay` for the panels and the closing stack they are ordered by, `@angular/cdk/a11y` for the two opposite halves of focus — the `FocusTrap` the dialog drives (decisions 0025 and 0029) and the `InteractivityChecker` the popover asks where its own tab order ends (decision 0031), a panel that takes focus without trapping it. The second name arrived with E1 and the second use of it with E2; this sentence changed with each — a reason that no longer describes the dependency is a permit nobody is reading. It is a peer because the consumer includes `@angular/cdk/overlay-prebuilt.css` themselves: a version they cannot see is a stylesheet they cannot match.

allowed.name: tslib
allowed.reason: The only runtime dependency, and nobody here typed it: `libs/components/package.json` declares no `dependencies` at all, and ng-packagr writes this one into the PACKED manifest when the library declares none, taking the range from `@angular/compiler`'s own manifest (lesson-64). It is not ceremonial — `importHelpers: true` in `tsconfig.base.json` makes the compiler emit its helpers as imports from `tslib` instead of a copy in every file that needs one.
allowed.unimported: Today no bundle imports it: at the target these sources compile to, nothing needs a helper. The entry says so out loud rather than letting the day one appears read as a new dependency — the declaration is right now, and the import may arrive at any change of the target.
